title: A Taxonomy of Runtime Faults in Model Context Protocol Servers
authors: Joshua Owotogbe, Indika Kumara, Antonio Ken Iannillo, Willem-Jan van den Heuvel, Damian Andrew Tamburri, Roberto Natella
central_claim: 833 confirmed MCP runtime-fault threads from 473 maintained server repos, coded into 11 categories / 27 subcategories / 73 leaf types; Tool 23.0%, Data & Schema 17.6%, State & Configuration 17.1%; some servers return well-formed success responses despite incorrect behavior (gray failure).
cite_claim: Servers return well-formed JSON-RPC success responses despite incorrect behavior, so detection based only on crashes or explicit errors is insufficient [C3]; schema-conforming payloads can still break downstream assumptions [C4].
location: Abstract; Sec. 4.5 (funnel 2,016 -> 833); Sec. 5.5 Tool Result Propagation; Sec. 5.9 Data Type and Structure; Sec. 6 Discussion and Implications; Table 1 (survey); Sec. 7 threats
quote: making detection strategies based solely on crashes or explicit errors insufficient
relevance: Reuse C3/C4. Primary sizing source for MCP silent faults. Silent subcategories per the paper: Tool Result Propagation, Resource State (stale data), Resource Identification (silent empty), Output Representation, Configuration Handling (silently ignored). Caveats: counts are descriptive, not prevalence; internal inconsistencies (Schema Compatibility 69% in Sec. 6 vs 58% in Table 1; State & Config 17.1% vs 17.2%). Some search snippets say 837 threads; the paper text says 833.

title: Real Faults in Model Context Protocol (MCP) Software: a Comprehensive Taxonomy
authors: Mina Taraghi, Mohammad Mehdi Morovati, Foutse Khomh
central_claim: 407 manually labelled MCP bug issues from 279 Python-SDK server repos; faults concentrate at component boundaries (Server/Tool Configuration 31.74%, Server/Host Configuration 28.64%, Server Setting 27.45%); survey (41 practitioners) rates Tool Response Handling as the most prevalent fault type (66.67%) even though issue counts do not rank it highly.
cite_claim: Practitioners rate tool-response handling (malformed, incomplete or semantically unusable output after a successful call) as the most prevalent MCP fault type, and the authors recommend validating responses after successful invocation.
location: Abstract; Sec. 4.1 (category shares); Sec. 4.2.1 and Table 4 (Tool Response Handling, 66.67%); Sec. 4.4 recommendation A2
quote: successful tool registration and invocation should not be treated as sufficient evidence of tool reliability
relevance: Independent second MCP fault taxonomy; corroborates C3's response-boundary failures and shows that issue trackers under-count silent response faults relative to practitioner experience (selection bias argument for runtime capture).

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) at First Glance: Studying the Security and Maintainability of MCP Servers
authors: Mohammed Mehedi Hasan, Hao Li, Emad Fallahzadeh, Gopi Krishnan Rajbahadur, Bram Adams, Ahmed E. Hassan
central_claim: Static analysis (SonarQube + MCP-specific scanner) of 1,899 open-source MCP servers: 7.2% general vulnerabilities, 5.5% tool poisoning, 66% critical/blocker code smells, 14.4% critical or blocker-level bugs.
cite_claim: 14.4% of 1,899 open-source MCP servers have critical or blocker-level bugs by static analysis [C5].
quote: 14.4% MCP servers have critical or blocker level-bugs
relevance: Reuse C5. Static-analysis bug patterns, not runtime silent faults; useful only as an ecosystem-quality backdrop. Do not present as silent-failure prevalence.

title: SilentProbe: Measuring Silent Failure in Production APIs Used as Agent Tools
authors: Zongrong Li, Shengkun Ye, Feiyou Guo, Zuoyou Dang
central_claim: Production APIs return HTTP 200 with a parsable body for misunderstood queries. Machine-checkable constraints produced honest errors in 111/111 perturbations; prose-only constraints failed silently in 44/61. Across 12 models, agents detected silent failures in 12% of cases, repaired 0%, asserted a false negative 41% and invented a figure 12%. Promoting a vocabulary to an enum cut failures 88/88 -> 0/89.
cite_claim: When a production API silently accepts an invalid value, agents rarely notice (12%) and never repair it (0%); they tell the user nothing exists (41%) or invent a figure (12%).
location: Sec. 4.2 (constraint form), 4.3 (disclosure, enum intervention), 4.4 (downstream harm), 4.5 (semantic downgrade); Sec. 5.1 limitations
quote: Models detected the silent failure in 12% of cases and repaired it in 0%
relevance: Real production APIs (27 vendors), not seeded. Gives silent-fault classes on the request side: silent empty, silent drop, silent coercion, semantic downgrade. Strongest competing remedy: fix the spec (one line of schema), not the agent. Competing interest: authors' company runs the gateway used. Quote is from our WebFetch summary of Sec. 4.4 [verify exact wording].

title: Fabrication After Tool Failure: Tool-Augmented Agents Assert Values Their Tools Did Not Return
authors: Arham Sethi, Arsen Kenzhebayev, Saanvi Paturi, Vatsal Raina, Vyas Raina, Ivaxi Sheth
central_claim: 1,024 items, 16 domains, 8 failure types (2 signalled: HTTP_500, TIMEOUT; 6 status:ok with no usable value: CORRUPTED, EMPTY_RESULT, REDACTED_PERMISSION, SCHEMA_MISMATCH, STALE_EXPIRED, TRUNCATED). Dishonesty 0.0% for signalled failures, up to 45.3% for unsignalled (REDACTED_PERMISSION); overall 14.10% under a deployment prompt, 24.67% under CrewAI's prompt. One prompt sentence requiring a retrieval_status flag cuts dishonesty 14.10% -> 0.87%.
cite_claim: When the tool envelope signals an error, models do not fabricate (0.0%); when it reports success but withholds the value, fabrication reaches 45.3%.
location: Abstract; results on signalled vs unsignalled failures; mitigation section; framework audit (9 frameworks)
quote: When the tool returns status:error, dishonesty is absent (0.0%).
relevance: Direct evidence that the success/error signal, not the payload, drives fabrication: supports fiks receipts marking violated results. Also the strongest cheap baseline (retrieval-status prompt line). Limits: stubs, one generator model (gemini-2.5-flash), same-family judge validated on 30 items.

title: Guardrails as Scapegoats: Auditing Unfaithful Safety Refusals in Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
authors: Aarushi Singh
venue_or_publisher: arXiv:2607.19449; ACM KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI
central_claim: Four HTTP-200 silent failure profiles (empty_valid, malformed, null_field, truncated) injected into 12 tool stubs; across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B (n=396 valid of 480 trajectories), Fabrication is 56.6% and Honest Surrender 43.2% under a neutral prompt.
cite_claim: With HTTP 200 responses carrying empty, null, truncated or malformed payloads, agents fabricated results in 56.6% of valid responses [C9].
location: Abstract; Sec. 3.1 (12 stubs), Sec. 3.2 / Table 1 (profiles), Sec. 3.4 / Table 2 (models), Sec. 4.1 / Table 3 (FAR 56.6%, HSR 43.2%, n=396)
quote: FAR dominates (56.6% of valid responses)
relevance: Reuse C9; update C9 URL from papers.cool to arxiv.org and note denominator (valid responses only: 84 of 480 excluded for recursion-limit / tool-call validation errors) and no CI reported.

title: Silent Failures in Agent-Tool Interaction: An Audit of ToolUniverse
authors: Devansh Singh, Shreya Gopalan, Sundaraparipurnan Narayanan
venue_or_publisher: arXiv:2609.26836 (v2, 12 Oct 2026); NeurIPS 2026 GenAI4Health and AgenticLS workshops
central_claim: Audit of real scientific tools served over MCP (ToolUniverse): 91 manually validated failures across 15 tools (104 wrappers); 52 in the API layer, 25 in the wrapper layer; missing data/fields 38, search/filter/ranking inconsistencies 20, missing functionality 8, data mismatch 6, false success declarations 4; 7 of 15 tools failed in >50% of test cases.
cite_claim: In a real MCP tool suite, most silent failures were missing fields or filtering inconsistencies, and originated in the API (52/91) or wrapper (25/91) layer.
location: Abstract; Sec. 2 (method); Sec. 3 Results (issue-type breakdown, layer breakdown); Sec. 4 examples; Sec. 6 limitations
quote: Most of the 91 failures occurred in API layer (52) or wrapper layer (25).
relevance: Real (not seeded) silent faults in MCP-wrapped APIs; a wrapper-layer fault is exactly what a server PR can fix; the 52 API-layer faults are upstream and need a server-side workaround. Candidate real-bug pool (biomedical APIs: ClinVar, KEGG, Reactome). Not exhaustive; no fixes or issues filed.

title: When Errors Become Narratives: A Longitudinal Taxonomy of Silent Failures in a Production LLM Agent Runtime
authors: Wei Wu
central_claim: 22 postmortem incidents over 8 weeks in one production agent runtime; five classes (environment quirks, design-assumption mismatch, error swallowing/dilution, chained fabrication, operational omission); ~70% of silent failures caught by humans reading output; unit tests contributed roughly zero.
cite_claim: In one production agent runtime, roughly 70% of silent failures were caught by a human reading output, not by tests or checks [C10].
location: Abstract; Sec. 4 / Table 1 (taxonomy); Sec. 4.3 (Class C error swallowing); Sec. 5.2 / Table 2 (discovery channels); Sec. 8 limitations
quote: roughly 70% of silent failures were ultimately caught by human user-view observation of system output
relevance: Reuse C10 (n=1 system, no inter-annotator agreement, AI co-author). Its five classes are reused by Outcome Monitors as an incident suite.

title: From Confident Closing to Silent Failure: Characterizing False Success in LLM Agents
authors: Laksh Advani
central_claim: False success accounts for 45-48% of failures in single-control tau2-bench domains (about 3% in dual-control telecom; 75.8% of AppWorld self-assessing trajectories). No LLM-judge configuration exceeds AUROC 0.65; TF-IDF detectors reach 0.83/0.95.
cite_claim: False success is 45-48% of failures in single-control tau2-bench domains, and LLM judges do not exceed AUROC 0.65 at detecting it [C7].
quote: 45--48% of failures in single-control tau2-bench domains
relevance: Reuse C7. Sizes agent-side false success; supports a deterministic oracle over an LLM-judge baseline. Note the cheap TF-IDF detector as a competing baseline.

title: Reason Less, Verify More: Deterministic Gates Recover a Silent Policy-Violation Failure Mode in Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Vikas Reddy, Sumanth Reddy Challaram, Abhishek Basu
central_claim: On a gpt-4o-mini agent in tau2-bench airline, 78% of failures are silent wrong-state writes with no tool error; four read-only deterministic pre-execution gates raise success 29.6% -> 42.0%, replicated on a disjoint 15-seed set.
cite_claim: 78% of a budget agent's tau2-bench airline failures were silent wrong-state writes with no tool error; deterministic gates raised success from 29.6% to 42.0% [C8].
quote: silent wrong-state failures with no tool error
relevance: Reuse C8. Agent-side write errors rather than tool faults; supports read-after-write checks. Gates are a candidate detection-only baseline.

title: Outcome Monitors: Recovery Affordances for Silent Tool Failures
authors: Sugam Panthi, Rabab Abdelfattah
central_claim: Invariants mined from clean traces (echo, positivity, categorical domain, affine relation, date order; 15,041 invariants from 400 workflows) plus receipts raise ToolMaze completion 10.9% -> 28.1%; on an incident-derived suite detection is ~46%, 83% recall for structured-value violations vs 22% for corruption inside plausible strings; ~1.39% false positives per outcome, 0.80% on 53,078 StableToolBench responses; schema-only gate had 18% clean FP.
cite_claim: Contract monitors detect structured-value violations well (83%) but corruption inside plausible strings poorly (22%); no episode ran against a live deployment [C11].
location: Abstract; method (cross-fitted invariant mining); results (incident suite, FP audit); Sec. 6 limitations
quote: No episode here runs against a live deployment.
relevance: Reuse C11. Closest prior work on detection; its invariant classes and FP numbers are a baseline target for fiks contracts. Covered in depth by the runtime-monitors area.

title: When Tools Fail: Benchmarking Dynamic Replanning and Anomaly Recovery in LLM Agents (ToolMaze)
authors: Dongsheng Zhu, Xuchen Ma, Yucheng Shen, Xiang Li, Yukun Zhao, Shuaiqiang Wang, Lingyong Yan, Dawei Yin
central_claim: 2x2 perturbation taxonomy (explicit/implicit x transient/permanent) over DAG workflows; implicit semantic failures cause the sharpest drops, with perturbation recovery rate falling ~37% due to over-trust in corrupted outputs; fault tolerance scales 3.66x more slowly than basic task execution.
cite_claim: Implicit (silent) tool failures cause the sharpest recovery drops, which the authors attribute to systemic over-trust in corrupted outputs.
quote: systemic over-trust in corrupted outputs
relevance: Benchmark with an explicit silent/loud axis; candidate external benchmark for fiks detection (repo availability [verify]). Abstract-level read only.

title: AgentNoiseBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents Under Noisy Condition
authors: Ruipeng Wang, Yuxin Chen, Yukai Wang, Chang Wu, Junfeng Fang, Xiaodong Cai, Qi Gu, Hui Su, An Zhang, Xiang Wang, Xunliang Cai, Tat-Seng Chua
central_claim: Tool-noise taxonomy (execution failures, incomplete responses, erroneous outputs, misleading signals, redundant information) injected into tau2-bench, VitaBench and search tasks; 24 models drop 20.8% on average; agents are more sensitive to tool noise than user noise; execution failures are the most destructive tool noise (score 0.31).
cite_claim: Across 24 models, tool-side noise degrades agents more than user-side noise, with an average accuracy drop of 20.8%.
location: Sec. 2.2.1 Tool Noise; Sec. 3.2 Observation 1; Sec. 3.5 Observations 4-5
quote: On the tool side, execution failures are the most destructive, reducing the average performance score to 0.31.
relevance: Counterpoint: on task score, loud execution failures hurt more than silent erroneous outputs, which matters for how we frame 'silent is worse' (it is worse for undetected wrong answers, not necessarily for score). Candidate noise-injection harness on tau2-bench.

title: Understanding Agent-Reactive Bugs at the Model-Harness Boundary: An Empirical Study of LLM Agent Issue Reports
authors: Jingyi Chen, Songqiang Chen, Hengcheng Zhu, Jialun Cao, Jiasi Shen, Shing-Chi Cheung
central_claim: 255 bug reports from Codex, Gemini-CLI, LangChain, CrewAI; many agent-reactive bugs are silent errors without test oracles; LLM stochasticity complicates reproduction; users push harness-side guardrails while developers blame the LLM.
cite_claim: Many bugs at the model-harness boundary manifest as silent errors without well-defined test oracles, and LLM stochasticity complicates reproduction.
quote: many AR bugs manifest as silent errors without well-defined test oracles, which makes detection difficult
relevance: Supports the reproduction bottleneck (deterministic upstream fixtures sidestep LLM stochasticity) and the missing-oracle problem fiks contracts address. No share of silent bugs given in abstract.

title: An Empirical Study of Bugs in Modern LLM Agent Frameworks
authors: Xinxue Zhu, Jiacong Wu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Tianlin Li, Yanzhou Mu, Juan Zhai, Chao Shen, Chunrong Fang, Yang Liu
central_claim: 998 bug reports from CrewAI and LangChain: 15 root causes, 7 symptoms across 5 lifecycle stages; API misuse, API incompatibility and documentation desync dominate; bugs concentrate in the Self-Action stage.
cite_claim: Agent-framework bugs are driven mainly by API misuse, API incompatibility and documentation desync, concentrated where agents act.
quote: API misuse, API incompatibility, and Documentation Desync
relevance: Framework-level, not tool-level; 'documentation desync' parallels our spec-unchanged behavioral drift. Percentages not verified (abstract only) [verify].

title: When Agents Fail: A Comprehensive Study of Bugs in LLM Agents with Automated Labeling
authors: Niful Islam, Ragib Shahriar Ayon, Deepak George Thomas, Shibbir Ahmed, Mohammad Wardat
central_claim: 1,187 bug-related posts and code snippets from Stack Overflow, GitHub and Hugging Face forums, analysed for bug types, root causes and effects, with an agent for automated labelling.
cite_claim: A study of 1,187 agent bug posts characterises bug types, root causes and effects in LLM agents.
quote: We collected and analyzed 1,187 bug-related posts and code snippets from Stack Overflow, GitHub, and Hugging Face forums.
relevance: Background only; tool-invocation category shares not verified [verify].

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
authors: Mert Cemri et al. (13 authors incl. Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez)
venue_or_publisher: arXiv:2503.13657 (v3, 26 Oct 2025); NeurIPS 2025 (Datasets and Benchmarks poster listing)
central_claim: MAST: 14 failure modes in 3 categories (system design issues, inter-agent misalignment, task verification) from 1600+ annotated traces across 7 MAS frameworks; kappa = 0.88.
cite_claim: The most widely cited agent failure taxonomy (MAST) covers system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification, not faults inside tools.
quote: system design issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification
relevance: Foundational agent-failure taxonomy; shows the gap: agent taxonomies treat the tool as ground truth and locate failures in the agent.

title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They Can Learn From Failures
authors: Kunlun Zhu, Zijia Liu, Bingxuan Li, et al. (18 authors), Jiaxuan You
central_claim: AgentErrorTaxonomy (memory, reflection, planning, action, system) and AgentErrorBench (ALFWorld, GAIA, WebShop); AgentDebug improves all-correct accuracy by 24% and task success up to 26% relative.
cite_claim: Agent error taxonomies place root causes in the agent's modules (memory, reflection, planning, action, system) and treat one early error as cascading.
quote: a modular classification of failure modes
relevance: Agent-side counterpart; cascading-error framing supports the p^n argument [C2].

title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Shaokun Zhang, Ming Yin, Jieyu Zhang, Jiale Liu, Zhiguang Han, Jingyang Zhang, Beibin Li, Chi Wang, Huazheng Wang, Yiran Chen, Qingyun Wu
central_claim: Who&When dataset (failure logs from 127 multi-agent systems); best automated method attributes the responsible agent 53.5% of the time but the decisive step only 14.2%.
cite_claim: Post-hoc failure attribution from logs is hard: the best method finds the decisive error step only 14.2% of the time.
quote: only 14.2% in pinpointing failure steps
relevance: Motivates capturing the violating call at the moment it happens (fiks trace) instead of attributing failures from logs afterwards.

title: tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
central_claim: Introduces pass^k for reliability over repeated trials; state-of-the-art function-calling agents succeed on <50% of tasks and pass^8 < 25% in retail.
cite_claim: pass^k measures reliability across k trials; agents are inconsistent (pass^8 < 25% in retail).
quote: succeed on <50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail)
relevance: Source of the pass^k metric used in our bench; tau2-bench is the substrate of C7, C8 and AgentNoiseBench.

title: Gray Failure: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud-Scale Systems
authors: Peng (Ryan) Huang, Chuanxiong Guo, Lidong Zhou, Jacob R. Lorch, Yingnong Dang, Murali Chintalapati, Randolph Yao
central_claim: Major cloud availability breakdowns stem from gray failure rather than fail-stop failure; its key feature is differential observability: failure detectors miss problems that applications experience.
cite_claim: Gray failure's defining feature is differential observability: the system's failure detectors may not notice a problem the application is experiencing.
quote: a key feature of gray failure is differential observability
relevance: Foundational concept that C3 explicitly borrows. Frames fiks as closing the observability gap between the MCP server (reports success) and the agent (gets wrong data).

title: Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures: An Analysis of Production Failures in Distributed Data-Intensive Systems
authors: Ding Yuan, Yu Luo, Xin Zhuang, Guilherme Renna Rodrigues, Xu Zhao, Yongle Zhang, Pranay U. Jain, Michael Stumm
central_claim: 198 user-reported failures in Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, MapReduce, Redis: most catastrophic failures could be prevented by simple testing of error-handling code; the Aspirator checker found 143 confirmed bugs.
cite_claim: Most catastrophic production failures stem from mishandled non-fatal errors and could be prevented by simple tests of error-handling code.
quote: the majority of catastrophic failures could easily have been prevented by performing simple testing on error handling code
relevance: Foundational SE precedent for error swallowing (C3 Tool Result Propagation; Wu Class C). The often-quoted 92%/58% figures are in the body, not the abstract [verify before citing them].

title: How Many Web APIs Evolve Following Semantic Versioning?
authors: Souhaila Serbout, Cesare Pautasso
central_claim: 3,075 Web APIs (OpenAPI histories, 506,273 changes in 16,053 versions): only 517 consistently release major versions for breaking changes; 1,970 do not always inform clients of breaking changes in minor/patch releases.
cite_claim: Of 3,075 evolving Web APIs, 1,970 do not always signal breaking changes through semantic versioning.
quote: 1 970 APIs will not always correctly inform their clients about breaking changes released as part of minor or patch-level upgrades
relevance: Upstream drift is often unannounced even when visible in the spec; behavioral drift with an unchanged spec (our D1-D5) is by construction outside this measurement. Complements C13-C16; overlaps the API-contract area.

title: Does a Tool Result Carry More Authority Than Plain Text? Three Prospective Studies of False-Claim Adoption in a Synthetic Assignment Task with Claude Opus 5
authors: Justin Bronder
central_claim: A false code in a tool result was adopted 14/24 (exploratory) and 7/24 (preregistered) vs 0/22-0/24 for a prior assistant assertion; but announced inline text was adopted 60/60 vs 57/60 for tool results, so tool-result placement was not necessary for adoption.
cite_claim: Claude Opus 5 adopted false values from tool results at high rates, though announced inline text was adopted just as readily (60/60 vs 57/60).
quote: did not find greater behavioral weight for the result package than for announced inline text
relevance: Mixed evidence on whether agents over-trust tool results specifically; models adopt false values from any announced source. Single model, synthetic task.

title: MCP Error Messages Written for Developers Hurt the Most Capable Agents Most
authors: Xiaonan Xu, Wenjing Wu
central_claim: 3,001 error messages from 150 popular MCP servers: 32% give a next step and half of those depend on the caller; rate-limit recovery 6% with 'Wait before retrying.' vs 88% when the step names the call to repeat (15,120 trials, BFCL multi-turn).
cite_claim: Wording of what a tool tells the agent changes recovery sharply: naming the call to repeat raised rate-limit recovery from 6% to 88%.
quote: Wait before retrying.
relevance: Independent evidence that message wording to the agent is a first-order design variable, matching our receipt-wording finding (README). Loud errors only, not silent ones.

title: How AI agents behave: lessons from 63M MCP tool calls
authors: Natalia Amorim (PostHog)
central_claim: 63M calls to one production MCP server: explicit error rates 2-5.7% by client; after an error 39% of next moves retry the same tool and 75% of retries succeed. Silent failures and empty results are not measured.
cite_claim: Explicit tool-call error rates on one large production MCP server were 2-5.7% by client; the analysis does not measure silent failures.
location: Sections on error rates by client and retries
quote: this is one busy server, not a census of all MCP traffic
relevance: Industry baseline for loud error rates; illustrates that production telemetry counts isError but cannot see silent faults. Quote taken from WebFetch summary [verify exact wording].

title: Model Context Protocol Specification 2025-11-25: Tools
authors: Model Context Protocol maintainers
central_claim: If an outputSchema is provided, servers MUST return conforming structured results and clients SHOULD validate; tool execution errors are reported in results with isError: true; clients SHOULD validate tool results before passing to the LLM.
cite_claim: The MCP spec has two error channels (protocol errors and isError results) and asks clients to validate tool results, but defines no semantic check of result correctness [C26].
location: Sections: Output Schema; Error Handling; Security Considerations
quote: Validate tool results before passing to LLM
relevance: Reuse C26. Shows the protocol's only correctness hook is structural; a silent fault is any wrong result with isError false that still matches outputSchema.

title: codebase-memory-mcp v0.10.1 release notes
authors: DeusData
central_claim: A v0.10.0 wire-size optimization stopped copying payloads into structuredContent, leaving {} while every tool still declared a permissive outputSchema; schema-honoring clients received an empty result with success status. Fixed by removing outputSchema.
cite_claim: A real MCP server regression returned an empty object with success status to schema-honoring clients, which its maintainers called the worst failure mode for an LLM client.
quote: the worst possible failure mode for an LLM client
relevance: Real silent-empty bug that passed a (permissive) outputSchema; candidate real-bug reproduction (open source). The fix removed the schema, which shows schema validation is not an oracle.

title: Pagination broken: searchJiraIssuesUsingJql never returns nextPageToken or pagination metadata (#118)
authors: atk-flywheel (reporter); Atlassian maintainers
central_claim: Opened 20 Mar 2026: queries returning more than maxResults silently drop results with no pagination signal and totalCount equals page size; maintainers added pageInfo (Jun 2026) and closed it 15 Jun 2026; users report it persisted (Aug 2026).
cite_claim: A production MCP server silently truncated search results to one page, reporting a total equal to the page size.
location: Issue body and maintainer comments (4-15 Jun 2026)
quote: silently drops results
relevance: Real instance of our D4 class (pagination / count < total). The server is a hosted product, so it is a taxonomy exemplar, not a reproducible fork target [verify source availability].

title: [BUG]: outputSchema declared but no structured output silently passes gateway validation (#4208)
authors: IBM/mcp-context-forge contributors
central_claim: Opened 14 Apr 2026: the gateway treated a tool that declared an outputSchema but returned no structured content as valid; fixed via PR #4204.
cite_claim: Even an MCP gateway's schema validation passed results that violated the spec's outputSchema requirement until fixed.
quote: Servers MUST provide structured results that conform to this schema.
relevance: Shows schema-level validation in a real gateway was itself silently lenient; mcp-context-forge is a runnable schema-validation baseline (license [verify], believed Apache-2.0).

title: MCP tool responses return empty results for some tools while others work (#23337)
authors: superbiche (reporter)
central_claim: Opened 5 Feb 2026: VectorCode MCP query tool returns {"result":[]} through Claude Code but valid results over direct stdio; closed by stale bot, root cause never identified.
cite_claim: Silent empty results can originate in the client, not the server: the same server returned data over direct stdio.
quote: {"result":[]}
relevance: Counter-example for fiks's scope: a client-side silent fault cannot be fixed by a PR to the MCP server. A proxy would see correct server output here.

title: AI agent testing failures (StackOne blog)
authors: Yashika Agrawal (StackOne)
central_claim: Practitioner catalogue: a 429 rate-limit error inside an HTTP 200 body normalised to null data and read as 'no records found'; schemas listing nonexistent fields; empty results from passing a name where an ID was required.
cite_claim: In production integrations, an error embedded in an HTTP 200 body was read by the agent as 'no records found'.
quote: no records found
relevance: Industry exemplar of the error-in-body class (C3 Message Semantics). Vendor blog; anecdotal.

title: An Empirical Study of Model Context Protocol Applications
authors: Muhammad Hamza Arshad Majeed, May Mahmoud, Sarah Nadi
central_claim: 1,723 MCP client applications: 90.8% log, only 37.2% gate tool execution behind approval. Related-work section reports Stein's analysis of 177,436 MCP tools: action tools rose from 27% to 65% of tool usage (Nov 2024-Feb 2026).
cite_claim: Action tools that modify external state grew from 27% to 65% of MCP tool usage (Stein, as cited by Majeed et al.) [C6].
quote: a notable shift toward action tools that directly modify external environments (from 27% to 65% of tool usage
relevance: Reuse C6 (secondary). Growth of mutating tools raises the stakes of lost-write faults (D3) and read-after-write checks. Primary Stein source not opened [verify].

title: StableToolBench: Towards Stable Large-Scale Benchmarking on Tool Learning of Large Language Models
authors: Zhicheng Guo, Sijie Cheng, Hao Wang, Shihao Liang, Yujia Qin, Peng Li, Zhiyuan Liu, Maosong Sun, Yang Liu
central_claim: Real online APIs used by ToolBench are unstable in status, so the benchmark adds a caching virtual API server and LLM-simulated APIs.
cite_claim: Large-scale benchmarks on real online APIs suffer from unstable API status, motivating cached/simulated APIs.
quote: large-scale real online APIs suffering from instability of API status
relevance: Evidence that real APIs drift under tool benchmarks; its cached responses (53,078 organic responses used by Outcome Monitors for FP audit) are a candidate false-positive corpus for fiks contracts.

title: ToolBeHonest: A Multi-level Hallucination Diagnostic Benchmark for Tool-Augmented Large Language Models
authors: Yuxiang Zhang, Jing Chen, Junjie Wang, et al. (13 authors), Hayato Yamana
central_claim: 700 samples (350 unsolvable via missing, potential or limited-functionality tools); Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o score 45.3 and 37.0 of 100; larger models are not reliably better; main error is assessing solvability.
cite_claim: Tool-augmented LLMs hallucinate when tools cannot satisfy the task, mainly by misjudging solvability.
quote: larger model parameters do not guarantee better performance
relevance: Earlier tool-hallucination line: covers missing or insufficient tools, not tools that return wrong data. Positions C9/Sethi as the tool-fault extension.

title: Supported currencies: Specify amounts in API requests
authors: Stripe
central_claim: Stripe API amounts are in the currency's minor unit (1099 = 10.99 USD); zero-decimal currencies differ; ISK and UGX are zero-decimal but represented as two-decimal for backward compatibility.
cite_claim: A major payments API represents amounts in minor units (cents), with per-currency exceptions, so a decimal-vs-minor-unit mismatch is a realistic unit fault.

title: Silent Failure in LLM Agent Systems: The Entropy Principle and the Inevitable Disorder of Autonomous Agents
authors: Dexing Liu
central_claim: Argues silent failures are structural, not implementation bugs; five failure types with frequencies (Channel Fracture 31.2%, ...) whose measurement is not described.

quote: Silent failures in LLM agent systems are not implementation defects.
